name: Reliabilism
statement: A belief is justified when it is produced by a reliable, truth-conducive process.
statementAccent: produced by a reliable, truth-conducive process
meaning: Reliabilism is an approach to epistemology that grounds justification and knowledge in the reliability, the truth-conduciveness, of the processes that produce our beliefs. In its best-known form, process reliabilism, a belief is justified when it is produced by a cognitive process that has a high truth-ratio, one that tends to produce a high proportion of true beliefs to false ones, such as normal perception, memory, or good reasoning. What matters is not that the believer can articulate reasons but that the belief-forming process is in fact reliable. Process reliabilism about justification was originally formulated by the philosopher Alvin Goldman in his 1979 paper What Is Justified Belief?, and its structure has a base clause, that beliefs produced by unconditionally reliable processes are justified, and a recursive clause, that beliefs produced by conditionally reliable processes, like inference, are justified when they operate on already justified inputs. Reliabilism is a paradigm form of externalism in epistemology, because it makes justification depend on a factor external to the believer's conscious mental states, namely the actual reliability of the process, which the believer may not be able to recognize or access by reflection. This sets it against internalism, on which justification depends only on factors internal to the person, such as their evidence or mental states. Reliabilism is motivated in part as a response to the Gettier problem and by the aim of a naturalistic epistemology.
mechanism: Reliabilism explains what makes a belief justified by looking at how the belief was produced rather than at what reasons the believer can give. On process reliabilism, the justificatory status of a belief depends on the reliability of the cognitive process that caused it, where a reliable process is one with a high truth-ratio, tending to yield far more true beliefs than false ones across the range of cases in which it operates. Perception in good conditions, memory, and sound reasoning are paradigm reliable processes; wishful thinking, guessing, and hasty generalization are unreliable. Goldman's account is recursive. A base clause covers belief-independent processes, such as perception, which take non-belief inputs and are justification-conferring when unconditionally reliable. A recursive clause covers belief-dependent processes, such as inference, which take beliefs as inputs and are conditionally reliable, conferring justification on their outputs when their inputs are themselves justified and the process is reliable in transmitting truth. Because the crucial factor, actual reliability, is a matter of the process's real-world track record and causal history, it lies outside the believer's introspective access, which is why reliabilism is a form of externalism: a belief can be justified even if the subject cannot cite any reason for it, provided it was reliably produced. This is what lets reliabilism attribute knowledge to young children and non-human animals who cannot articulate justifications, and lets it address Gettier cases and fit a naturalized picture of knowledge without unreduced epistemic notions.

examples.text: A belief formed by normal vision in good light is justified because vision is a reliable, truth-conducive process.
A belief can be justified even if the subject cannot cite reasons, provided it was reliably produced, unlike on internalism.
Reliabilism lets young children and animals count as knowing, since their beliefs can be reliably produced without articulated reasons.

variants.name: Process reliabilism
variants.text: Goldman's account on which justification depends on the truth-ratio of the belief-forming process, with base and recursive clauses.

variants.name: Externalism versus internalism
variants.text: Reliabilism makes justification depend on external reliability, against internalism's demand for accessible internal grounds.

whyItMatters: Reliabilism is one of the most influential theories in contemporary epistemology and the leading form of externalism about justification. By locating justification in the truth-conduciveness of belief-forming processes rather than in reasons the believer can articulate, Goldman's 1979 account launched what has been called the reliabilist revolution and reframed the whole debate between internalism and externalism. Reliabilism has several attractions that keep it central. It offers a response to the Gettier problem by tying justification to processes that reliably connect belief with truth; it fits a naturalistic epistemology, explaining justification without appeal to unreduced epistemic notions and connecting the theory of knowledge to cognitive science; and it extends knowledge naturally to young children and non-human animals, who plainly know things yet cannot state their reasons. The theory also sharpens the internalism-externalism dispute, forcing internalists to say why accessible grounds should be required and externalists to handle cases where reliability and internal evidence come apart. Its central problems, the generality problem, the new evil demon problem, and the clairvoyance cases, are themselves landmarks of the field.

working.text: ask which cognitive process produced the belief, such as perception, memory, or inference.
count the belief justified if the process has a high truth-ratio, reliably yielding true beliefs.
let justification depend on actual reliability, not on reasons the believer can access or articulate.

limits: Reliabilism faces three well-known challenges. The generality problem is the difficulty of specifying which process it is whose reliability determines justification, since any particular belief is produced by a token process that instantiates many process-types, broad and narrow, with different reliability levels, and the theory needs a principled way to pick the relevant type. The new evil demon problem, raised by Stewart Cohen with Keith Lehrer in the early 1980s, imagines a victim in a demon world whose beliefs are formed by processes internally identical to ours but, because the world deceives them, are unreliable; intuitively such a subject's beliefs seem just as justified as ours, yet reliabilism must deny it, which suggests justification tracks internal factors reliability misses. The clairvoyance cases, due to Laurence BonJour around 1980, describe someone, Norman, with a perfectly reliable clairvoyant faculty but no evidence that he has it; intuitively Norman is not justified in his clairvoyant beliefs, yet reliabilism implies he is, suggesting reliability without accessible evidence is not enough.
misreadings: Reliabilism is not the view that a believer must know or show that their process is reliable; as an externalist theory it holds that actual reliability confers justification whether or not the subject can access it. It is not the same as requiring good evidence in the internalist sense, since a reliably produced belief can be justified without articulated reasons. And it does not claim reliable processes are infallible, only that they have a high truth-ratio, so treating reliabilism as demanding awareness of reliability, as a form of evidentialism, or as requiring infallibility, misreads a leading externalist account of justification.
origin: An externalist approach to epistemology, formulated by Alvin Goldman in his 1979 paper What Is Justified Belief?, on which a belief is justified when produced by a reliable, truth-conducive cognitive process.

(1979), its base and recursive clauses, its status as a paradigm externalism, and the generality problem.

Internalism and Externalism in Epistemology, Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the internalism/externalism distinction, reliabilism as making justification depend on external reliability the subject may not recognize, and the challenges including the new evil demon and BonJour's clairvoyance case.
